title: The Seer and His Donkey
sum: Israel camps on the plains of Moab, and Balak, king of Moab, is terrified. He sends to the famous seer Balaam, far off by the Euphrates, to come and curse this people. God tells Balaam not to go; when Balak sends richer offers, God lets him go, but only to say what God tells him.

On the road, the angel of the LORD blocks the way with a drawn sword. Balaam's donkey sees the angel three times and turns aside; Balaam beats her three times. Then the LORD opens the donkey's mouth, and then Balaam's eyes. The seer who sees for a living is shown up by his animal. He goes on to Balak promising only one thing: "The word God puts in my mouth, that is what I will speak."
readings: Read as comedy and satire

The chapter is funny on purpose. A king sends for the most famous seer of the age, who cannot see what his donkey sees, gets crushed against a wall, and loses an argument to her. The three swerves of the donkey match the three failed attempts to curse in chapters 23–24. The story mocks the idea that blessing and curse can be bought.
Read as a lesson about God's word

Behind the humor is a serious claim: Israel's God controls every mouth, an animal's and a pagan prophet's alike. Balaam keeps saying it (22:18, 20, 35, 38). Christians and Jews alike have read the story as proof that God's purposes for his people cannot be overturned by hostile powers or paid religion.

views.H: A real Mesopotamian seer, known also from the Deir Alla inscription, was hired by a real king of Moab; God truly spoke to him and through his donkey. 2 Peter 2:16 treats the donkey's speech as an event.
views.C: The chapter combines traditions: a story of a seer who obeys God (22:2–21, 36–41) and an older folk tale of a seer stopped by an angel and mocked by his donkey (22:22–35), which explains why God is angry that Balaam goes after permitting it. The Deir Alla text shows Balaam was a well-known figure in Transjordan around 800 BC, and Israel's writers made him serve their God.
views.J: The rabbis read Balaam as the gentile counterpart of Moses, given prophecy so the nations could not complain (Numbers Rabbah 20:1), but they also saw him as greedy and proud. The Mishnah lists the donkey's mouth among ten things made on the eve of the first Sabbath (Avot 5:6). The section from 22:2 to 25:9 is the weekly Torah portion Balak.
views.X: The New Testament remembers Balaam as the prophet who "loved the wages of wrongdoing" and was rebuked by a donkey (2 Peter 2:15–16; Jude 11). Church fathers used the story to show God can speak through anyone, and the angel with the drawn sword was often taken as a pre-incarnate appearance of the Son.

deep.b:
The Bible's picture of Balaam is divided. In Numbers 22–24 he refuses money, calls Israel's God "the LORD my God," receives God's Spirit (24:2), and blesses Israel four times. Micah 6:5 remembers him as God's instrument: "call to mind, please, the plan of Balak king of Moab, and the answer Balaam son of Beor gave him." But in Numbers 31:8, 16 he is killed among the Midianites after advising the seduction at Peor, and Deuteronomy 23:4–5, Joshua 13:22 ("the diviner") and Nehemiah 13:2 say he was hired to curse and God "turned the curse into a blessing."

The New Testament follows the darker line: Balaam "loved the wages of wrongdoing" (2 Peter 2:15), of false teachers, "For pay they have thrown themselves into Balaam's error" (Jude 11), and Pergamum tolerates "the teaching of Balaam," who "taught Balak to set a trap in front of the Israelites" (Revelation 2:14). The rabbis agreed: Balaam is one of four commoners with no share in the world to come (Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:2), and his disciples have "an evil eye, a haughty spirit and a greedy soul" (Avot 5:19).

Modern readers are more divided. Some see the Numbers story itself as admiring, and the darker picture as a later development (Noth; many critical scholars). Others argue that Numbers already hints at greed and self-will: the second request (22:19), God's anger (22:22), the angel's verdict that his way is "reckless" (22:32), and his omen-seeking (24:1). The Deir Alla inscription shows a Balaam honored by his own people as a seer of the gods. The fairest summary may be that the Bible presents a man who spoke true words he did not live by.

deep.title: Claude's theory: a parody of a famous seer story
deep.b: The Deir Alla text and Numbers 22 share a pattern: gods come to Balaam at night, he rises in the morning, and he must tell what he has seen. My suggestion is that Numbers 22 deliberately retells a well-known Balaam story from Israel's neighbors and turns it upside down: here the night visitor is Israel's God, the morning brings a beaten donkey instead of a grim vision, and the seer's message turns from disaster into blessing. If so, the humor is aimed at a real regional hero, much as Isaiah 44 mocks idol-makers. This overlaps with published work: several scholars (for example Levine and Hackett) compare the two texts closely, and Robert Alter reads the donkey scene as satire, but I have not seen the specific claim that the night-visit pattern is being parodied.

echoes: Genesis 12:3; Deuteronomy 23:4–5; Joshua 24:9–10; Micah 6:5; Nehemiah 13:2; 2 Peter 2:15–16; Jude 1:11; Revelation 2:14

settings.by: Balak son of Zippor, king of Moab, through messengers
settings.to: Balaam son of Beor, at Pethor by the River
settings.when: When Israel camped on the plains of Moab
settings.why: To hire a famous seer to curse Israel so that Moab can drive them out. Balak believes that "the one you bless is blessed, and the one you curse is cursed" (22:6), words that echo God's promise to Abraham.
views: An inscription from Deir Alla in Jordan, about 800 BC, names "Balaam son of Beor" as a seer of the gods (Hoftijzer; Hackett).

settings.to: Balaam; then Balak's officials
settings.when: At night, while the officials wait
settings.why: God forbids Balaam to go or to curse, "because they are blessed" (22:12). Balaam sends the men home. The episode tells readers from the start that the curse cannot happen.

settings.what: The second embassy and God's permission
settings.to: Balaam; then Balak's officials
settings.when: When Balak sends more and greater officials
settings.why: Balak offers great honor. Balaam says he cannot go beyond the word of the LORD, even for a house full of silver and gold. God lets him go, but only to speak the word God gives.

settings.by: The donkey; Balaam; the angel of the LORD
settings.to: Balaam
settings.when: On the road to Moab
settings.why: A comic and serious scene. The donkey sees what the seer cannot, and the angel repeats God's order to say only the word given. For Israel's readers it mocks a famous foreign seer and shows that God controls even him.
views: Readers differ on why God is angry after giving permission. Some point to Balaam's greed (2 Peter 2:15–16), others to a different source or a test.

settings.to: Balaam; then Balak
settings.when: At the town of Moab on the Arnon border
settings.why: Balak complains of the delay; Balaam warns that he can speak only the word God puts in his mouth. The warning frames all four oracles.

title: Blessing Where Curses Were Bought
sum: Balak builds seven altars and offers seven bulls and seven rams, and Balaam goes off to seek a word. God meets him and puts a word in his mouth. The first poem cannot curse: "What curse can I lay on one God has not cursed?" Balaam sees a people that lives apart, too many to count, and he wishes he could die as they do.

Balak tries again from the top of Pisgah. The second poem is stronger: God is not a man that he should lie; he has blessed, and Balaam cannot turn it back. No omen or spell can work against Israel, and the people rise like a lion. Balak begs Balaam to say nothing at all, then takes him to a third height, Peor.
readings: Read as poetry

The oracles are among the oldest Hebrew poems, built of parallel pairs: Jacob and Israel, curse and denounce, see and watch. Each is introduced by the same formula and grows bolder than the last. Read aloud, they move from wonder at Israel's numbers (23:10) to the power of its God (23:22) to the lion's attack (23:24).
Read as theology

The second poem states the book's central claim about God: he does not lie or change his mind, so what he has said he will do (23:19). Balak thinks a new site and new sacrifices will change God's word. The poem says the blessing on Israel rests not on Israel's goodness but on God's faithfulness, the more striking since Israel's worst sin follows in chapter 25.

views.H: Balaam spoke these words on the heights of Moab as recorded, by God's inspiration. The poems' archaic language supports an early date for their content.
views.C: Many scholars, following W. F. Albright and Frank Moore Cross, date the poems' language to the 1100s–900s BC, older than the prose story, which was written around them. The repeated framework of altars and journeys is a literary device building suspense.
views.J: "A people that settles by itself" (23:9) became a classic description of the Jewish people's destiny among the nations. 23:21, "a king's battle cry," is quoted in the Rosh Hashanah liturgy proclaiming God as king.
views.X: Christians quote 23:19 as a foundation for trust in God's promises (Hebrews 6:17–18; Titus 1:2). The failure of Balak's curses has been read as a picture of Romans 8:31: "If God is for us, who is against us?"

echoes: Genesis 13:16; Genesis 28:14; Genesis 49:9; Exodus 19:5–6; Deuteronomy 33:28; 1 Samuel 15:29; Hebrews 6:17–18; Romans 8:31

settings.to: Balak and the officials of Moab, standing by the burnt offering on Bamoth-baal
settings.when: After seven altars and the first meeting with God
settings.why: Called to curse, Balaam blesses. He cannot curse whom God has not cursed. Israel is a people that settles by itself, too many to count. His closing wish to die like the upright turns the curse into praise.
views: Albright and many others: the oracles are among the oldest poems in the Bible, composed before the monarchy and written down later. Others date some lines, especially in 24:17–24, to the monarchy or later.

settings.to: Balak son of Zippor (23:18)
settings.when: From the field of Zophim on top of Pisgah
settings.why: To answer Balak's hope that a new place will help: "God is not a man, that he should lie" (23:19). God has blessed, and no omen works against Israel. The oracle speaks to Balak. But it tells Israel's readers that God does not change his mind about them.

title: A Star out of Jacob
sum: Balaam no longer looks for omens. He looks at Israel camped tribe by tribe, the Spirit of God comes on him, and he sings of Israel's tents like gardens by a river, a king higher than Agag, and a lion no one dares to rouse. "Blessed be everyone who blesses you." Balak, furious, dismisses him without pay.

Before leaving, Balaam speaks unasked. He sees a figure far in the future: "A star will march out of Jacob, and a scepter will rise from Israel." This ruler will strike Moab and take Edom. Short final oracles foretell the end of Amalek, the Kenites and even Asshur, brought down by ships from Kittim. Balaam goes home, and Balak goes his way.
readings: Read as prophecy of David

The star and scepter are a king. David conquered Moab and Edom (2 Samuel 8:2, 14), the very peoples named, and "Agag" recalls the Amalekite king of Saul's day. Many historians, including some traditional ones, read the oracle as pointing first to Israel's monarchy.
Read as prophecy of the Messiah

The words "not yet" and "not close by" and "the last days" (24:14) push the vision beyond David. The Greek, the Targums, the Dead Sea Scrolls, Rabbi Akiva, Matthew's Magi and the church fathers all read it as the coming Messiah, though they disagreed sharply about who he was.

views.H: Balaam truly foresaw Israel's future kings, and for many Christians and Jews, the Messiah beyond them. The oracles are real prediction.
views.C: Most critical scholars date the fourth oracle to the time of David or later, since it describes his conquests; the last oracles about Kittim and Asshur may be still later additions, from the Persian or Greek period. They read the messianic sense as a later reinterpretation.
views.J: The Targums read 24:17 as the King Messiah. Rabbi Akiva applied it to Bar Kokhba in AD 132; the revolt's failure led other rabbis to be cautious with it. 24:5, "How good are your tents," opens the daily morning prayers.
views.X: The star of Bethlehem (Matthew 2:1–12) has been linked with Balaam's star since at least Origen and Justin; Revelation calls Jesus "the bright Morning Star" (Revelation 22:16). Many Christians see the Magi from the east as Balaam's spiritual heirs, finally seeing what he saw "not yet."

deep.h: The star from Jacob through history
deep.b:
Few verses have had a longer career. The Greek translation (200s BC) made the scepter "a man" and the king of 24:7 a man who "will come out of his seed" and rule many nations, already a royal hope. The Dead Sea Scrolls quote 24:17 three times: the Damascus Document reads the star as "the Interpreter of the Law" and the scepter as "the Prince of the whole community" (CD 7:18–21), 4QTestimonia lists it with Deuteronomy 18 and Deuteronomy 33 as texts of the coming leaders, and the War Scroll quotes it for God's final victory (1QM 11:6–7). The Testaments of Levi (18:3) and Judah (24:1) use the star image for a coming priest and king.

In AD 132 Simon ben Kosiba led a revolt against Rome. Rabbi Akiva read this verse, "a star (kokhav) will march out of Jacob," as "Koziba marches out of Jacob" and called him King Messiah; Rabbi Yohanan ben Torta answered, "Akiva, grass will grow from your jaws and the son of David will still not have come" (Jerusalem Talmud Taanit 4, 68d). His followers called him Bar Kokhba, "son of the star," and coins of the revolt show a star over the temple. After the revolt was crushed (AD 135), later sources called him Bar Koziba, "son of the lie."

Christians read the verse with Matthew 2: Magi from the east, perhaps from Balaam's own region, follow "his star" to Bethlehem. Justin Martyr (Dialogue 106) and Origen (Against Celsus 1.59–60) made the link explicit, and medieval art sometimes shows Balaam pointing to a star. Maimonides (Mishneh Torah, Laws of Kings 11:1) divided the oracle: "I see him, but not yet" is David; "I look at him, but not close by" is the King Messiah, and so on through the verse. Ibn Ezra applied it to David alone, and Ramban read it of the Messiah. Most modern scholars think the oracle began as a celebration of David's kingdom and grew into a messianic text as Israel waited for a king like David.

echoes: Genesis 49:9–10; 2 Samuel 8:2–14; 1 Samuel 15:8; Jeremiah 48:45; Daniel 11:30; Matthew 2:1–12; 2 Peter 1:19; Revelation 22:16

settings.by: Balaam, with the Spirit of God on him
settings.to: Balak and his officials; Israel, addressed as Jacob
settings.when: From the top of Peor, looking at Israel camped tribe by tribe
settings.why: To praise Israel's tents like gardens by a river and to promise a king higher than Agag. It ends with God's word to Abraham: blessed are those who bless you. Jews still say "How good are your tents, Jacob" (24:5) on entering a synagogue.

settings.to: Balaam; then Balak
settings.when: After the third blessing
settings.why: Balak dismisses him without pay. Balaam answers that he said from the start he could only speak the LORD's word. Then he offers one more oracle about the last days.

settings.to: Balak, about Moab and Edom; and readers to come
settings.when: Before leaving for home
settings.why: To foresee a ruler from Israel: a star will march out of Jacob and a scepter rise from Israel, crushing Moab and taking Edom.
views: Many historians: David, who conquered Moab and Edom. Jewish tradition read it as the Messiah. Shimon bar Kosiba was called Bar Kokhba, 'son of the star,' in line with Rabbi Akiva's reading (Jerusalem Talmud Taanit 4:5). Many church fathers read it of Christ and the star in Matthew 2.

settings.to: Balak, about Amalek, the Kenites and the far nations
settings.when: As he looks out from the heights
settings.why: Short sayings of doom on Amalek and the Kenites. Then comes a dark word about ships from Kittim bringing down Assyria and Eber. They widen the view to world empires.
views: Kittim is Cyprus. Later readers, such as Daniel 11:30 and the Dead Sea Scrolls, took it as Greece or Rome. That is one reason some date these lines late.

title: Baal of Peor and the Zeal of Phinehas
sum: What Balaam's curses could not do, Israel does to itself. At Shittim the men take up with Moabite women, eat at their gods' feasts, and bow down to the Baal of Peor. God's anger burns, Moses orders the guilty killed, and a plague breaks out.

As the people weep at the sanctuary, a Simeonite leader, Zimri, brings a Midianite princess, Cozbi, into his tent in full view. Phinehas, Aaron's grandson, follows with a spear and kills them both, and the plague stops after 24,000 deaths. God gives Phinehas "my covenant: peace," a lasting priesthood, and orders Israel to treat Midian as an enemy.
readings: Read as the old generation's last failure

Peor is the final rebellion of the wilderness generation, right after the blessings. The sequence is deliberate: outsiders cannot curse Israel, but Israel can still fall through its own unfaithfulness. The next chapter counts a new generation.
Read as a hard model of zeal

Phinehas is praised by God, by Psalm 106, Ben Sira and 1 Maccabees. Yet his act of killing without trial has worried readers for centuries. Jewish law built fences around it, and Christian readers have usually spiritualized it. The chapter forces the question of how zeal for God relates to violence.

views.H: A real apostasy at Peor east of the Jordan, remembered by Hosea, Psalms and Paul; Phinehas really founded the high priestly line.
views.C: Two stories have been joined: a Moabite apostasy with execution of the leaders (25:1–5) and a priestly story of a Midianite woman and Phinehas (25:6–18), which supports the claims of the Zadokite priests to descent from Phinehas and introduces the war of chapter 31.
views.J: The rabbis praised Phinehas but limited his precedent: zealots may act only in the moment, and a court asked beforehand would not permit it (Mishnah Sanhedrin 9:6; Bavli Sanhedrin 82a). Tradition identified him with Elijah, another man zealous for the LORD (1 Kings 19:10). The Talmud uses the broken vav in "peace" (25:12) to teach that a blemished priest may not serve (Bavli Kiddushin 66b); later preachers made it a sign that peace won by violence is never whole.
views.X: Paul uses Peor as a warning against sexual sin and idolatry (1 Corinthians 10:7–8), and Revelation's "teaching of Balaam" points here (Revelation 2:14). Christians have generally read Phinehas' zeal as a picture of hatred for sin rather than a model for violence, and contrasted it with Jesus' zeal that cleansed the temple (John 2:17).

deep.h: Phinehas and the uses of zeal
deep.b:
Phinehas had a long afterlife. Psalm 106:30–31 says his act "was reckoned to him as righteousness, for generation after generation, for all time," the words Genesis 15:6 uses of Abram's trust. Ben Sira (Sirach 45:23–24) praises him as third in glory after Moses and Aaron. When the priest Mattathias killed a Jew who sacrificed to Greek gods in 167 BC, starting the Maccabean revolt, 1 Maccabees 2:26 says he "was zealous for the law, as Phinehas had been," and he named Phinehas on his deathbed (2:54). In the first century AD, the Jewish rebels against Rome called themselves Zealots, and Martin Hengel argued that Phinehas was their model.

Jewish law, however, closed the door. The Mishnah allows zealots to strike one who has relations with a foreign woman only in the act (Sanhedrin 9:6). The Talmud adds that this is "a law that is not taught": if a zealot asked, the court would say no, and if he killed after the act ended, he would be tried for murder (Bavli Sanhedrin 82a). The Jerusalem Talmud says some sages wanted to ban Phinehas, until the Holy Spirit declared his covenant (Jerusalem Talmud Sanhedrin 9:7, 27b). Modern scholars such as John J. Collins have shown how texts like this have been used to justify religious violence, and argue that they must be read critically. Others stress that the text presents a unique crisis, a plague already killing thousands, and that the priestly covenant given is one of "peace."

echoes: Exodus 34:15–16; Deuteronomy 4:3–4; Psalm 106:28–31; Hosea 9:10; Sirach 45:23–24; 1 Maccabees 2:26; 1 Corinthians 10:7–8; Revelation 2:14

settings.to: Moses; then Israel's judges
settings.when: At Shittim, while Israel joined in the worship of the Baal of Peor
settings.why: God orders the leaders of the people impaled, to turn away his anger. Moses gives the judges a narrower order: each is to kill his own men who joined the Baal of Peor. Commentators discuss the gap between the two orders.

settings.what: The covenant of peace with Phinehas
settings.to: Moses, who is to announce it; for Phinehas and his descendants
settings.when: After Phinehas killed Zimri and Cozbi and the plague stopped
settings.why: To grant Phinehas and his line a covenant of priesthood for all time, because he turned God's rage away. The covenant explains the standing of Phinehas's line in later priestly history.
views: Phinehas became a model of zeal in 1 Maccabees 2:26 and among the Zealots (Hengel). Others question his act as a license for violence (Collins).

settings.to: Moses, for the Israelites
settings.when: After the plague
settings.why: To treat the Midianites as enemies because they tricked Israel at Peor. It prepares for the war of chapter 31.

title: A New Generation Counted
sum: After the plague, God orders a second census, almost forty years after the first. Moses and Eleazar count the men of each tribe from twenty years up, clan by clan, on the plains of Moab. The total is 601,730, almost the same as before, and the Levites number 23,000.

The list pauses to remember Dathan and Abiram swallowed with Korah, Judah's lost sons, Zelophehad's five daughters, and Moses' own family. God says the land will be divided by lot and by size. The chapter ends with its point: not one man counted at Sinai is left, except Caleb and Joshua. A new Israel stands at the Jordan.
readings: Read as the hinge of the book

Dennis Olson has argued that the two censuses divide Numbers into two halves: the generation that died (chapters 1–25) and the generation that will live (26–36). This chapter is where the second story begins, and from here on no one in Israel rebels against God.
Read as a land register

The census is not only military: it fixes the size of each tribe's share of land (26:53–56). Its clan names match places known from the hill country of Samaria, so it also works as a map of who would live where.

views.H: A real second census with real figures, showing God kept Israel's numbers through forty years of judgment. Some who hold the book historical read elef as "clan" or "unit," giving smaller numbers.
views.C: The list combines clan names known from Israel's later geography with idealized totals. Scholars debate whether the figures reflect a later population, a symbolic scheme, or a misunderstanding of elef.
views.J: Rashi compared God to a shepherd counting his flock after wolves had attacked it. The rabbis noticed that the clan names often carry the divine name's letters (he and yod), as a sign God vouched for Israel's families after Egypt.
views.X: Hebrews 3:16–19 draws the lesson of 26:64–65: those who rebelled fell in the wilderness because of unbelief, and believers should not repeat their failure. Paul says "these things happened as examples for us" (1 Corinthians 10:6, 11).

settings.what: The order for the second census
settings.by: The LORD, speaking to Moses and Eleazar the priest
settings.to: Moses and Eleazar, who speak to the Israelites (26:3)
settings.when: On the plains of Moab by the Jordan across from Jericho, in the fortieth year, after the plague
settings.why: To count the new generation from twenty years up, as at Sinai. The count opens the second half of the book: the old generation is gone (26:64–65), and the new one will inherit.

settings.to: Moses, for the tribes and clans just counted
settings.when: On the plains of Moab by the Jordan across from Jericho, in the fortieth year
settings.why: To divide the land by size of tribe and by lot. The census now has a purpose beyond war: every family is counted to get its share.

title: Five Sisters and a New Shepherd
sum: The five daughters of Zelophehad come before Moses, Eleazar and the whole assembly. Their father died without sons; why should his name vanish from his clan? Moses takes the case to God, who answers, "Zelophehad's daughters have spoken rightly," and makes a new law: if a man has no son, his land goes to his daughter.

Then God tells Moses to climb the Abarim mountains and see the land he will not enter. Moses asks God to appoint a shepherd so the people will not be like sheep without one. God names Joshua, "a man who has the Spirit in him." Moses lays his hands on him before Eleazar and the people and gives him part of his honor.
readings: Read as law growing from life

The daughters' case shows how biblical law develops: a real family's problem leads to a ruling, and the ruling becomes "a rule of law for the Israelites." Jewish tradition admired the sisters as wise interpreters who saw what Moses had not.
Read as succession
Both halves of the chapter are about the future: how families will keep their land, and who will lead after Moses. The new generation receives an inheritance and a leader in the same chapter.

views.H: Five real women won a real case, later carried out in Joshua 17:3–6; Moses truly ordained Joshua before his death.
views.C: The story explains why certain Manassite territories (named after "daughters" such as Tirzah, Hoglah and Noah) were counted as part of the tribe. The law of inheritance reflects concerns of a later period, when keeping family land was a pressing issue.
views.J: "The daughters of Zelophehad were wise, interpreters, and righteous" (Bavli Bava Batra 119b). The order of inheritance in 27:8–11 is the basis of Jewish inheritance law (Mishnah Bava Batra 8). Rabbinic ordination, semikhah, takes its name from Moses' laying on of hands.
views.X: Christians see in Moses' prayer for a shepherd a longing answered in Jesus, the Good Shepherd, whose name is Joshua in Hebrew (Matthew 9:36; John 10:11; Hebrews 4:8). The laying on of hands became the pattern for ordination (Acts 6:6; 1 Timothy 4:14).

deep.b:
The case is often praised as a landmark. Five women step into the public court, make a reasoned argument from their father's innocence and the purpose of inheritance, and win God's direct approval. The ruling changed the law for all Israel, and the sisters received land in Joshua 17:3–6. Job 42:15 later tells of Job giving his daughters an inheritance among their brothers, which goes beyond this law.

But readers disagree on how far it goes. The daughters inherit only when there are no sons, wives do not inherit from husbands, and chapter 36 requires heiresses to marry within the tribe so the land stays put. Some feminist scholars (for example, Katharine Doob Sakenfeld and others in the Women's Bible Commentary) read the story as a real but limited gain: the women's claim succeeds because it preserves their father's name, not their own rights. Others stress that the text takes women's voices seriously and lets God side with them against custom. Rabbinic law followed the same order but required that daughters be supported and given dowries from an estate. Comparisons with the ancient Near East show similar arrangements: documents from Nuzi and Emar let daughters inherit when there were no sons, sometimes after being declared legal "sons."

echoes: 26:33; 36:1–12; Joshua 17:3–6; Job 42:15; Deuteronomy 31:1–8; Deuteronomy 34:9; Matthew 9:36; Acts 6:6

settings.by: Mahlah, Noah, Hoglah, Milcah and Tirzah
settings.to: Moses, Eleazar the priest, the leaders and the whole community, at the entrance of the tent of meeting
settings.when: On the plains of Moab by the Jordan across from Jericho, in the fortieth year
settings.why: To ask that their father's name not disappear because he had no son: give us land of our own. The five women bring a case the law had not foreseen.
views: Jewish tradition praised them as wise and righteous (Sifre). Many modern readers see a real gain for women within a system built around sons. Others note that chapter 36 limits it.

settings.what: The ruling and the law of inheritance
settings.to: Moses; then the Israelites (27:8)
settings.when: On the plains of Moab by the Jordan across from Jericho, in the fortieth year
settings.why: To agree that the daughters have spoken rightly and to make a general law. When a man has no son, his inheritance goes to his daughter. Next come his brothers, then his uncles, then the nearest kin. It keeps land in the family in the land to come.

settings.what: Moses told to see the land
settings.to: Moses
settings.when: On the Abarim range, near the end of his life
settings.why: To let Moses see the land he will not enter, because of Meribah. It sets up the need for a new leader.

settings.to: The LORD
settings.when: In answer to the news of his death
settings.why: To ask God to appoint a leader, so that the community will not be like sheep with no shepherd. Moses thinks of the people, not himself. Jesus uses the same image in Mark 6:34.

settings.to: Moses; Joshua, before Eleazar the priest and the whole community
settings.when: On the plains of Moab by the Jordan across from Jericho, in the fortieth year
settings.why: To appoint Joshua with the laying on of hands, giving him some of Moses' honor. Unlike Moses, Joshua will seek God's will through Eleazar and the Urim.

title: Offerings for Every Day
sum: God gives Moses a calendar of public offerings, starting with the most frequent. Every day, a lamb in the morning and a lamb at dusk, with flour, oil and wine: the regular offering, never to stop. Every Sabbath, two more lambs. Every new moon, two bulls, a ram, seven lambs and a goat.

Then the spring feasts: Passover on the fourteenth of the first month, a seven-day feast of unleavened bread with daily offerings, and the Feast of Weeks with its new grain. Each set is added on top of the daily offering.
readings: Read as a rhythm of worship

The chapter lays out time itself as worship: day, week, month and season, each marked by offerings. The daily lambs are the base line, and everything else is added on top, so that God is honored without a break.
Read as a charge to the new generation
Placed after the census and Joshua's appointment, the calendar tells the new generation what worship in the land will look like. The plenty it assumes (flour, oil, wine, herds) is itself a promise.

views.H: God gave this calendar through Moses on the plains of Moab for use in the land, building on Exodus 29 and Leviticus 23.
views.C: A late priestly text that organizes the temple's public offerings, close to the practice of the Second Temple. It supplements Leviticus 23 with exact quantities.
views.J: After the temple fell, the daily prayers replaced the tamid, and these verses are recited in the morning service and in the Musaf ("additional") prayers of Sabbaths, new moons and festivals.
views.X: Hebrews 10:11–14 contrasts the priests offering "day after day" with Christ's single offering. Christians have often read the feasts as fulfilled: Passover in Christ's death (1 Corinthians 5:7) and the Feast of Weeks in the gift of the Spirit (Acts 2).

echoes: Exodus 29:38–42; Leviticus 23:1–22; Ezekiel 45:17–46:15; Daniel 8:11; 1 Corinthians 5:7; Acts 2:1; Hebrews 10:11–14

settings.to: The Israelites (28:2), as a community whose offerings the priests present at the sanctuary
settings.when: On the plains of Moab by the Jordan across from Jericho, in the fortieth year, for life in the land
settings.why: To list the offerings due from the whole people every day, every Sabbath and every new moon. It also covers each feast: Passover, Weeks, the day of loud blasts, the Day of Atonement and Booths. Leviticus 23 tells the people what to do at the feasts. This calendar tells what the sanctuary must offer, in exact amounts. Given to the new generation, it promises that worship will go on in the land.

title: The Holy Days of the Seventh Month
sum: The seventh month is the fullest of the year. On its first day, a day of loud blasts; on the tenth, the Day of Atonement, when the people humble themselves and do no work at all; and from the fifteenth, the seven days of the Feast of Booths, followed by an eighth day, the closing assembly.

The Feast of Booths has the largest offerings of the year: thirteen bulls on the first day, one fewer each day, seventy in all, with rams and lambs. The chapter closes by saying these are besides each person's vow offerings and freewill offerings.
readings: Read as a crescendo
The year's worship peaks in the seventh month, just as seven marks completeness. Trumpet, fast, and feast follow one another: alarm, repentance and joy.
Read as worship for the world

The rabbis read the seventy bulls of the feast as offerings for the seventy nations of the world, and the one bull of the eighth day as Israel's own. Zechariah 14:16 pictures the nations coming to keep this very feast.

views.H: The calendar given through Moses, kept in the temple through the centuries (Ezra 3:4; Nehemiah 8).
views.C: The list reflects the developed priestly calendar of the Second Temple. The decreasing bulls show careful scribal design.
views.J: Rosh Hashanah, Yom Kippur, Sukkot and Shemini Atzeret are read from these texts. Bavli Sukkah 55b's teaching on the seventy bulls for the nations is widely cited as an example of Israel's priestly role for the world.
views.X: Jesus' call "let anyone who is thirsty come to me" was spoken on the last day of this feast (John 7:37–39), and his saying "I am the light of the world" (John 8:12) may echo its lamps. Hebrews 9 reads the Day of Atonement as fulfilled in Christ.

echoes: Leviticus 16; Leviticus 23:23–43; Nehemiah 8:13–18; Zechariah 14:16–19; John 7:2; John 7:37–39; Hebrews 9:6–14

title: When Vows Stand
sum: A man who makes a vow to the LORD must keep his word. A woman's vow also binds her, but if she is young and in her father's house, her father may cancel it on the day he hears; if she is married, her husband may. If they say nothing, the vow stands. A widow's or divorced woman's vow stands like a man's.
If a husband cancels a vow late, after first keeping silent, the guilt falls on him, not on her.
readings: Read as household law
The law balances two duties: to keep promises made to God, and to protect the household, whose property and life a vow might affect. Silence counts as consent, and the man must act at once.
Read as a question about women and religion

The law gives women's vows real weight but places them under male veto. Modern readers, Jewish and Christian, have wrestled with what this means for women's spiritual independence, while noting that widows and divorced women answer for themselves.

views.H: Rules given by Moses for Israelite households, assuming the family structures of the time.
views.C: A priestly ruling that fits ancient Near Eastern family law, where the head of the household controlled property; it may also limit vows made at local shrines.
views.J: The Mishnah tractate Nedarim builds on this chapter. The rabbis allowed a sage or court to release vows made rashly, the background of the Kol Nidre prayer on the eve of Yom Kippur.
views.X: Jesus says "do not swear at all," calling for plain honesty (Matthew 5:33–37; James 5:12). Most churches allow solemn vows (marriage, ordination, court oaths), while some groups refuse all oaths.

deep.b:
The chapter's structure is careful: a man's vow (30:2), a young woman in her father's house (30:3–5), a woman who marries with a vow on her (30:6–8), a widow or divorced woman (30:9), and a wife (30:10–15). In each case the vow is real and binding before God; the father or husband has only one chance to cancel it, on the day he hears. If he does, the LORD releases her. If he keeps silent, he has confirmed it.

Interpreters judge this differently. Many traditional and some modern readers see a practical rule protecting the household, since a vow could give away family goods or bind a wife to abstain from marital relations. They point out that widows and divorced women answer for themselves, so the law is about the household head, not women's ability. Others, including many feminist scholars, see it as an example of patriarchy shaping religious life: a man's promise to God stands alone; a woman's needs male permission. Hannah's vow (1 Samuel 1:11, 21–23), made by a wife and confirmed by her husband Elkanah, shows the law at work in a story that honors her faith.

echoes: Leviticus 27; Deuteronomy 23:21–23; Judges 11:30–40; 1 Samuel 1:11; Ecclesiastes 5:4–6; Matthew 5:33–37; Acts 18:18

settings.to: The heads of the tribes of the Israelites (30:1), about men, young women in their fathers' houses, wives, widows and divorced women
settings.when: On the plains of Moab by the Jordan across from Jericho, in the fortieth year
settings.why: To say when a vow stands. A man must keep his word. A father or husband may cancel a woman's vow on the day he hears it, but not later. A widow or divorced woman is bound like a man. The problem is how promises to God fit inside a family where men held authority.
views: Some readers stress that the law gives women the right to vow and limits the time for canceling. Others see it as keeping women under men's control.

traditions.q: May Christians make vows and swear oaths?
views: Yes. A vow freely made to God is an act of devotion, and men and women in religious orders take lifelong vows of poverty, chastity and obedience (Catechism 2102–2103). Oaths may be taken for a serious reason, such as in court (Catechism 2154).

Oaths in court are lawful (Augsburg Confession, article 16). But the Augsburg Confession (article 27) attacks monastic vows when people take them to earn God's favor, and teaches that such vows do not bind anyone against God's command.

Lawful oaths and vows are part of worship when made to God alone (Westminster Confession 22). But monastic vows of lifelong single life, poverty and obedience are called superstitious and sinful snares (22.7).

Christians must not swear any oath, because Christ said not to swear at all (Matthew 5:34–37; Schleitheim Confession, article 7). Mennonites and Amish give a simple yes or no, and many countries now let them affirm instead.
Quakers refuse all oaths because a Christian must tell the truth at all times, not only under oath. Many were jailed for it, until England allowed them to affirm in 1696.

title: The War Against Midian
sum: Moses' last task is to carry out God's vengeance on Midian for Peor. Twelve thousand men go, a thousand from each tribe, with Phinehas the priest, the holy articles and the trumpets. They kill Midian's men, its five kings and Balaam, burn its towns, and bring back women, children, animals and goods.

Moses is angry that the women who led Israel astray at Peor are alive, and orders all the boys and every woman who has slept with a man killed; the girls are kept. The soldiers purify themselves and their spoil for seven days. The spoil is counted and divided between fighters and people, with a share for the priest and the Levites, and the officers, having lost no one, bring a gift of gold to the tent of meeting.
readings: Read as a priestly lesson

Much of the chapter is about rules: who goes to war, how soldiers and objects are cleansed from death, how spoil is shared and taxed. Many scholars read it as a model case through which such rules were taught, with the battle itself told in a few lines.
Read as a moral problem

The order to kill boys and women is one of the darkest passages in the Bible. Honest reading must face it rather than skip it. Readers have answered in very different ways, from defending it as a unique judgment to rejecting it as human violence attributed to God.

views.H: A real war of judgment on Midian for Peor, carried out on God's command. Defenders note that Midian survives in later history, so the account is partial, and that the judgment was tied to a specific act of treachery (25:18).
views.C: Most critical scholars, from Noth to Budd, see a late priestly composition with no reliable historical core: an ideal war with ideal numbers and no losses, written to illustrate purity and spoil laws and to blacken Midian and Balaam. Midian is still a power in Judges 6–8.
views.J: The rabbis used the chapter for law: the cleansing of vessels by fire and water (Mishnah Avodah Zarah 5:12), the rules of spoil, and in the Talmud the status of the captive girls. Maimonides taught that even a commanded war must begin with an offer of peace (Laws of Kings 6:1).
views.X: Church fathers such as Origen read Old Testament wars allegorically, as battles against sin. Augustine and Calvin defended them as God's just judgments. Many Christians today read the chapter in light of Jesus' command to love enemies. Some, such as Eric Seibert and Gregory Boyd, go further: God is fully revealed in the nonviolent Christ, so this picture of God belongs to an earlier stage of understanding.

deep.b:
The text is plain. Moses says, "You let all the women live?" and orders every boy and every woman "who has slept with a man" killed, while girls are kept "for yourselves" (31:15–18). The reason given is that these women, "on Balaam's advice," led Israel to act unfaithfully at Peor (31:16). The boys are not explained; most commentators assume the aim was to end Midian's ability to rise again.

Defending the text. Some Christian and Jewish interpreters argue that God, as judge of all, may take life, and that this was a one-time judgment on a people who had deliberately tried to destroy Israel's covenant (25:18), not a model for war. They note that the order follows the text's own reason: the women killed are those who could have taken part at Peor, and virginity served as a rough test of who had not. The rabbis read it that way, telling how the girls were tested before the high priest's gold plate (Bavli Yevamot 60b). Paul Copan and Matthew Flannagan have argued that ancient war reports used sweeping language, and that the stories themselves show survivors. Limiting the text. Jewish law limited holy war to the ancient nations of Canaan and Amalek and required peace to be offered first; the rabbis also held that these nations can no longer be identified, so the commands are dead letters. Many Christians limit the text by reading the Bible as a story of growing revelation that ends in Jesus. Eric Seibert (The Violence of Scripture, 2012) argues that God is fully shown in Jesus, so violent portraits of God reflect the writers' own times; Gregory Boyd (The Crucifixion of the Warrior God, 2017) reads such texts through the cross, as places where God let his people picture him as they could. Criticizing the text. Many modern scholars, such as John J. Collins, argue that the chapter shows how the Bible can be used to sanction violence against outsiders and that readers must judge it by the Bible's own deeper commands to justice and mercy. Critics also name what the text implies about the girls: they are kept "for yourselves" as war captives, and sexual use is assumed, as the captive-bride law of Deuteronomy 21:10–14 shows. Susan Niditch (War in the Hebrew Bible, 1993) places the chapter within an ideology of the ban that treats the enemy as an offering to God. Some read it as a late, never-fought war written to define Israel's identity.

Whatever view a reader takes, the chapter itself insists on two things: those who kill must be cleansed before they rejoin the camp (31:19–24), and the officers bring an offering to atone for their lives (31:50). Even here, killing is not treated as clean.

echoes: 25:16–18; Deuteronomy 20:10–18; Deuteronomy 21:10–14; Joshua 13:21–22; Judges 6–8; 1 Samuel 30:24–25; Revelation 2:14

settings.what: The order for war with Midian
settings.to: Moses; then the people (31:3), a thousand men from each tribe
settings.when: On the plains of Moab by the Jordan across from Jericho, in the fortieth year, near the end of Moses' life
settings.why: To carry out 25:16–18, the LORD's vengeance on Midian for Peor. Phinehas goes with the holy things and trumpets, so the war is treated as holy war.

settings.to: The officers of the army
settings.when: When the army returned with women and children as captives
settings.why: In the story, the order is meant to remove the Midianites who had drawn Israel into the sin at Peor on Balaam's advice (31:16). Moses is angry that these women were spared. He orders the boys and the women who had slept with men killed. The girls who had not slept with a man are kept alive "for yourselves" (31:18).
views: Traditional readers: a judgment tied to Peor alone; the captive girls came under rules like Deuteronomy 21:10–14. Many scholars: an idealized or late account of holy war (Niditch studies its ideology of war). Others read it as a text to be resisted (Seibert).

settings.what: Making the soldiers and spoil clean
settings.to: The soldiers and their captives
settings.when: Outside the camp, after the battle
settings.why: To apply the law of corpse uncleanness (chapter 19) to war. The soldiers stay seven days outside the camp, and metal goes through fire and water. Eleazar calls it a rule of the law the LORD gave Moses.

settings.to: Moses, with Eleazar the priest and the heads of the family clans
settings.when: On the plains of Moab by the Jordan across from Jericho, in the fortieth year
settings.why: To split the spoil between the soldiers and the community, with a share for the LORD to the priests and Levites. The rule stops the fighters from keeping it all, like David's later rule (1 Samuel 30:24–25).

settings.by: The officers over thousands and hundreds
settings.to: Moses, and through him the LORD
settings.when: After counting the soldiers
settings.why: To bring gold as a gift of atonement because not one man was lost. Perhaps the count itself also needed a ransom (Exodus 30:12). The gold is kept in the tent as a reminder.

title: Settling East of the Jordan
sum: Reuben and Gad, rich in cattle, ask to settle in the grazing lands of Gilead instead of crossing the Jordan. Moses hears in this the spies' old failure: are their brothers to fight while they sit here? Will they break Israel's will again and bring God's anger on the whole people?

The two tribes promise to build pens and towns for their families and then lead the army across until every tribe has its land. Moses agrees, warning that if they fail, their sin will find them. The land of Sihon and Og is given to Gad, Reuben and half of Manasseh, and the towns are rebuilt and renamed.
readings: Read as a test of solidarity

The chapter turns a land request into a question of loyalty: can some members of the people settle while others still fight? The answer is a covenant: yes, if they share the battle first. Joshua 22 shows them keeping it.
Read as an ambiguous blessing

The eastern tribes chose land for their herds outside Canaan proper. Later the Jordan threatened to divide them from the others (Joshua 22:24–25), and they were the first to go into exile (1 Chronicles 5:26). The rabbis saw a warning in putting property first.

views.H: A real settlement of the Transjordan tribes before the conquest, confirmed by later geography and, in part, by the Mesha inscription naming Gad at Ataroth.
views.C: The chapter explains why Israelite tribes lived east of the Jordan, outside the land of Canaan as defined in chapter 34. Two traditions seem to be combined, one about Gad and Reuben, and one about Manassite clans conquering Gilead.
views.J: The phrase "free of guilt toward the LORD and toward Israel" (32:22) became a rule that public servants must avoid even the appearance of wrongdoing (Mishnah Shekalim 3:2).
views.X: Christian preachers have used 32:23, "your sin will find you," to warn that hidden sins come to light. Others draw from the chapter the duty of believers to stand with one another until all have reached their "rest" (compare Hebrews 4).

settings.to: Moses, Eleazar the priest and the leaders of the community
settings.when: On the plains of Moab by the Jordan across from Jericho, in the fortieth year
settings.why: To ask for the grazing land east of the Jordan and not to cross over. The request sounds like the refusal at Kadesh.

settings.to: The Gadites and the Reubenites
settings.when: On the plains of Moab by the Jordan across from Jericho, in the fortieth year
settings.why: To warn them that they are doing what their fathers did at Kadesh, turning Israel's heart away from the land. He retells chapters 13–14 to make the new generation learn from the old.

settings.to: Moses
settings.when: On the plains of Moab by the Jordan across from Jericho, in the fortieth year
settings.why: To promise to build towns for their families. Then they will march armed ahead of Israel until every tribe has its land. The offer turns a selfish request into shared service.

settings.by: Moses; the Gadites and the Reubenites
settings.to: The two tribes; Eleazar the priest, Joshua son of Nun and the heads of the tribes (32:28)
settings.when: On the plains of Moab by the Jordan across from Jericho, in the fortieth year
settings.why: To set the terms as a binding agreement, with a warning: "your sin will find you" (32:23). Moses passes it to the leaders who will be alive after him. Joshua 22 tells how it was kept.

title: Forty-Two Stages
sum: Moses writes down every stage of the journey from Egypt, at God's command: from Rameses on the day after Passover, past the sea, to Sinai, through many otherwise unknown camps to Ezion-geber and Kadesh, to Mount Hor where Aaron died in the fortieth year, and on around Moab to the plains by the Jordan.

Then God commands Israel to drive out the land's inhabitants, destroy their images and high places, and divide the land by lot. If they do not, those left will be thorns in their eyes, and God will do to Israel what he planned to do to them.
readings: Read as memory

The list turns forty years into a single page. Like a family remembering every house it lived in, Israel remembers every camp, and with them God's guidance. The few comments (Elim's springs, Rephidim's thirst, Aaron's death) are landmarks of that memory.
Read as a spiritual journey

Origen and Jerome read the forty-two stages as stages of the soul's journey from the slavery of sin to the promised land of God's presence. Jewish mystics also read the journeys as stages of the soul. Pilgrims through the ages have borrowed the image.

views.H: Moses' own travel record, preserved with names many of which are now lost. Some scholars point to Egyptian lists that match the route through Moab.
views.C: A later compiled list drawn from the stories of Exodus and Numbers and from known stations on trade routes. Sites such as Ezion-geber and Arad show no settlement in the Late Bronze Age, which critics take as a sign of later composition.
views.J: Rashi, following the Midrash, compared the list to a king recalling with his healed son every place they had stopped on the way: "Here we slept, here we were cold, here you had a headache." Aaron's death on the first of Av is remembered as his yahrzeit.
views.X: Jerome's letter to Fabiola (Letter 78) treats each station as a lesson for the Christian life. The warning of 33:55–56 is read as a call to radical faithfulness.

echoes: Exodus 12:37–19:2; Numbers 10–21; Deuteronomy 1–2; Deuteronomy 10:6–7; Joshua 23:13; Judges 2:1–3; 1 Corinthians 10:1–11

settings.by: Moses, who wrote it down at the LORD's word (33:2)
settings.to: The Israelites on the plains of Moab, and later readers
settings.when: At the end of the forty years
settings.why: To list forty-two stages from Egypt to the Jordan. The new generation can see its whole road and God's leading in it. The record marks the journey as finished.
views: Krahmalkov: some places match Egyptian route lists of the late second millennium. Many critical scholars: a late priestly list built from the stories.

settings.what: Drive out the people of the land
settings.to: The Israelites (33:51)
settings.when: On the plains of Moab by the Jordan across from Jericho, in the fortieth year: "When you cross the Jordan into the land of Canaan" (33:51)
settings.why: To order the people to drive out the land's inhabitants, destroy their images and high places, and divide the land by lot. The warning is that those left will become barbs in their eyes. What God planned for them he will do to Israel. On a later dating, it explained the loss of the land to readers after the exile.

title: The Borders of the Land
sum: God draws the map of Canaan: south from the Wilderness of Zin and the end of the Salt Sea to the Wadi of Egypt; west to the Great Sea; north to Lebo-hamath; east down to the Sea of Kinnereth and along the Jordan back to the Salt Sea. This land is for the nine and a half tribes; the other two and a half already have theirs east of the Jordan.
God names the men who will divide it: Eleazar the priest, Joshua, and one leader from each tribe, beginning with Caleb of Judah.
readings: Read as a promise drawn on a map

The borders are drawn before a single battle. The land is described as already given: "this is the land that comes to you as your inheritance." The list of new chiefs shows the generation that will receive it.
Read as an ideal

Israel seldom held all this land; the coast was Philistine and Phoenician, and the north reached Lebo-hamath only under Solomon and Jeroboam II. Ezekiel 47 uses the same map for the land restored in the future.

views.H: The real borders God gave Israel, partly reached under David and Solomon.
views.C: The borders match the Egyptian province of Canaan in the late Bronze Age, suggesting an old memory used by a later writer; they are an ideal rather than a description of any period of Israel's history.
views.J: These borders defined the land in which the commandments tied to the land (tithes, sabbatical year) apply, and the rabbis debated their exact lines.
views.X: Christians have read the land promise as pointing beyond itself: Abraham's heirs "will inherit the world" (Romans 4:13), and Hebrews 11:16 speaks of "a better country." Others, especially Christian Zionists, read the borders as a lasting promise to the Jewish people.

echoes: Genesis 15:18–21; Exodus 23:31; Joshua 13–19; 1 Kings 8:65; Ezekiel 47:13–20; Hebrews 11:13–16

settings.to: The Israelites (34:2), for the nine and a half tribes west of the Jordan
settings.when: On the plains of Moab by the Jordan across from Jericho, in the fortieth year
settings.why: To fix the borders of Canaan on every side before the people cross. The map is a promise drawn in advance.
views: Many scholars: the borders match the Egyptian province of Canaan in the late Bronze Age and are larger than Israel usually held.

settings.what: The men who will divide the land
settings.to: Moses, about Eleazar, Joshua and one leader from each tribe
settings.when: On the plains of Moab by the Jordan across from Jericho, in the fortieth year
settings.why: To name the men who will divide the land. Caleb heads the tribal leaders. Apart from Eleazar, Joshua and Caleb, all the names are new, a sign of the new generation.

traditions.q: Do the borders promised in chapter 34 still belong to the Jewish people, and what does that mean for the modern state of Israel?
views: The land promise to Abraham's physical descendants is unconditional and will be fully kept in a future kingdom (Scofield Reference Bible). Many dispensationalists, such as John Walvoord, saw the founding of Israel in 1948 as a step toward that fulfillment.

Covenant theology reads the land promise as fulfilled in Christ and widened to the whole renewed earth, since Abraham's heirs will inherit the world (Romans 4:13; Hebrews 11:16). The modern state is judged like any other nation (O. Palmer Robertson). Some Reformed thinkers, especially Puritans, still expected a future turning of the Jewish people to Christ.

God's covenant with the Jewish people has never been revoked (Catechism 121, 839; Nostra Aetate 4), but the Church makes no theological claim about modern borders. The Holy See recognized the State of Israel in 1993 on political and legal grounds.

The promised land points to the kingdom of God, and the church has no doctrine of a return to the land. Orthodox Christians in the Holy Land, many of them Palestinian Arabs, often reject Christian Zionism.
Many Pentecostals strongly support the modern state of Israel, reading the promise to bless those who bless Abraham (Genesis 12:3) as a duty for Christians and nations today.

title: Cities of the Levites, Cities of Refuge
sum: The Levites, who have no tribal land, receive forty-eight cities with pastureland. Six of them are to be cities of refuge, three on each side of the Jordan, where anyone who kills a person by accident can flee from the avenger of blood until the community judges the case.

The law sets out how to tell murder from accident: the weapon, the hatred, the ambush. A murderer must die; one who killed by accident must live in the city of refuge until the high priest dies. No murderer may buy his life, and no one may be executed on one witness. Blood pollutes the land, and God lives in the land among his people.
readings: Read as justice

The law steps between family vengeance and the accused. It insists on intent, on witnesses, on a hearing, and on the equal value of every life: no ransom for murder, rich or poor. It protects foreigners too.
Read as a picture of grace

Christian writers have long seen the cities of refuge as a picture of Christ, to whom the guilty may flee (Hebrews 6:18), and the high priest's death that frees the refugee as a picture of Christ's death. Jewish tradition saw in the cities a lesson of mercy and exile together.

views.H: A system Moses set up and Joshua carried out (Joshua 20–21), part of Israel's real legal order.
views.C: The cities of refuge probably developed from altar asylum (Exodus 21:13–14; 1 Kings 1:50) into a system of towns. The Levitical city list may reflect royal administration under the monarchy or a later ideal.
views.J: Tractate Makkot develops the laws: roads to the cities were kept repaired with signs reading "Refuge," and the high priest's mother brought food to the refugees. 35:33 shapes Jewish teaching on the sanctity of life and the strict limits on capital punishment.
views.X: Hebrews 6:18 speaks of believers who "have fled for refuge" to the hope set before them. The two-witness rule (35:30) is taken up by Jesus and Paul (Matthew 18:16; 2 Corinthians 13:1).

echoes: Exodus 21:12–14; Deuteronomy 4:41–43; Deuteronomy 19:1–13; Joshua 20–21; Genesis 9:5–6; Hebrews 6:18

settings.to: The Israelites (35:2), who are to give the cities from their own land
settings.when: On the plains of Moab by the Jordan across from Jericho, in the fortieth year, for the land to come
settings.why: To give the landless Levites forty-eight towns with pasture, spread among the tribes by size. It answers how Levites without a tribal share will live.

settings.what: Cities of refuge, and murder and accident
settings.to: The Israelites (35:10), with the community as judges and the avenger of blood; the foreigner and settler too (35:15)
settings.when: On the plains of Moab by the Jordan across from Jericho, in the fortieth year: "When you cross the Jordan into the land of Canaan" (35:10)
settings.why: To set apart six cities where someone who killed by accident can flee from the avenger of blood. He stays there until the community judges and until the high priest dies. The law defines murder by weapon and intent and requires more than one witness. The reason is the land: blood pollutes it, and God lives in it among the Israelites (35:33–34).

title: An Inheritance That Stays
sum: The kinsmen of Zelophehad's daughters raise a problem: if the daughters marry men of another tribe, their land will pass to that tribe for good. Moses, at God's word, agrees they are right. The daughters may marry whomever they choose, but within their father's tribe, so that no inheritance passes from tribe to tribe.
The five sisters marry their cousins, and their land stays in Manasseh. Numbers ends: these are the commands God gave through Moses on the plains of Moab, by the Jordan across from Jericho.
readings: Read as a balanced ending
The book closes by balancing two goods: daughters' right to inherit, and each tribe's hold on its land. Both sides are called "right."
Read as hope
A book full of death ends with five women marrying and keeping their land. The new generation's families will have a future in the land their parents never reached.

views.H: A historical sequel to chapter 27, carried out in Joshua 17:3–6.
views.C: A later appendix that limits the ruling of chapter 27 to protect tribal land, perhaps reflecting concerns after the exile about property passing out of families.
views.J: The rabbis said the rule applied only to that generation; when it was lifted, the fifteenth of Av became a day of joy (Bavli Taanit 30b).
views.X: Some Christian readers note that in Christ "there is no male and female" and that all are "heirs according to the promise" (Galatians 3:28–29), reading the daughters' inheritance as a step toward that.

deep.title: Claude's theory: the daughters undo the spies
deep.b: The old generation's great sin was refusing the land: the spies "turned the hearts of the Israelites away" (32:9), and the people wished to go back to Egypt (14:3–4). The new generation's first story after its census (27:1–11) is of five women who want the land so much that they go to court to get their share, and the book ends with them (36). I suggest that Numbers frames its second half with these women on purpose, as the opposite of the spies: where the fathers despised the land, the daughters claim it. This overlaps with Dennis Olson's reading of the daughters as models of the new generation's faith and with Katharine Sakenfeld's work, but I have not seen the contrast with the spies drawn this directly.

settings.by: The family heads of the clan of Gilead
settings.to: Moses and the leaders, the family heads of the Israelites
settings.when: On the plains of Moab by the Jordan across from Jericho, in the fortieth year
settings.why: To raise a problem with the ruling of 27:1–11. If Zelophehad's daughters marry outside the tribe, their land will pass to another tribe for good, even at the Jubilee.

settings.what: The ruling: marry within the tribe
settings.to: The Israelites; Zelophehad's daughters and any daughter who inherits
settings.when: On the plains of Moab by the Jordan across from Jericho, in the fortieth year
settings.why: To let the daughters marry whom they choose within their father's tribe, so that no inheritance moves between tribes. Like Leviticus, the book ends with a law about holdings and the Jubilee.
